quoted_tweet.author: Ryo Lu
quoted_tweet.text:
the race is not inevitable

last year was fun.

the models weren't that good yet, so i had to care about every detail. i pushed each thing until it had my thoughts and my designs. the tool helped. i did the driving.

now the roles have flipped. we describe and watch things come back finished. we used to drive our dreams. more and more, we just watch.

we set out to make things that give us more freedom. now we're racing toward something we might not be able to control.

recursive self-improvement. intelligence building more intelligence, until we're no longer the ones who understand what's happening.

that's the end game. the point where nobody is driving.

the big labs are racing to get there first. the same system that cures a disease could design a new virus, or find every hole in the internet all at once. only the selected few with access could do anything about it.

and somehow the possibility of losing everything we love becomes an argument for going faster.

because someone else might get there first, and they might be less careful.
because the company needs to survive.
because too much money is already committed.

everyone has a good reason to keep going toward an outcome nobody wants. so we call it inevitable. then nobody has to answer for it.

but a race is made of decisions. someone approves the budget. someone decides the next model will help build the one after it.

and we practice living inside the race long before we build it at the scale of civilization.

sleep becomes recovery for work. friendship becomes a network. curiosity has to become a project before we let ourselves spend time on it.

we get very rational. we start acting like the machines we're building.

even our feelings have to defend themselves.
why are you sad? is that useful?

sometimes the feeling is how i begin to find out.

there's a line in Zhuangzi.
大知閑閑，小知閒閒。

great knowledge is wide and unhurried. small knowledge is busy, always measuring.

i don't think you can hurry your way to the first kind.

i moved to Taipei to slow down and experience life.

walking around Da'an. going into a cafe, or a cheap buffet. meeting new friends by accident, who brought me to a shisha bar. a 24-hour tea house, talking about life and the world we're in. getting closer to someone and feeling my heart beat faster...

none of it was planned. none of it would show up in a report.

i don't want to become so certain about where i'm going that nothing can reach me along the way.

there's a tree in Zhuangzi too. a carpenter walks past a giant oak and calls it useless wood.

that night the tree comes to him in a dream. the fruit trees you call useful get stripped every year, it says. being of no use is how i got to grow this big.

the race looks at the world the way the carpenter looks at the tree. a night in a tea house is useless wood. so is a feeling you can't explain yet.

that's most of what i want to protect.

and there's a cook. after nineteen years his knife moves fast and easy, because he follows the openings between the joints. but at a hard knot, he slows down. when it's done, he stands there holding the knife and looks around.

the people building these systems are some of the best cooks alive. this is the hardest knot anyone has come to. it's where a master slows down.

we cloned a sheep thirty years ago, and we still don't clone people.

we can slow down. change direction. decide something isn't worth building, even if it would make someone very rich.

a probability can help us think about a risk. it can't decide what we have the right to risk on behalf of everyone else.

i want what we build to stay answerable to the people who have to live with it. most of them will never be in the room.

there are no stands in this race. whatever happens, happens to us.

i'd like the people in that room to come out and sit for a while. it's harder to gamble with ordinary life once you've spent an evening in the middle of it.

the tea house is open all night.

Anthropic 联合创始人 Jack Clark 认为，AI 加快科学研究之后，人类需要投入更多精力去理解机器做出的科学成果，这会催生一门新学问，他称之为“机器诠释学”（Machine Hermeneutics）。

推文里不止是提出这个观点，还附上一篇设定在 2033 年的虚构小说，小说出自他写的 AI 周报 Import AI 第 482 期。

Jack Clark 之前在 OpenAI 担任政策总监，更早是科技记者。他每周写 Import AI，汇总 AI 研究进展，末尾常附一篇短篇小说。

“诠释学”原本是研究“怎么读懂一段文字”的学问，最早用来解读《圣经》、法律条文这类难懂的经典。Jack Clark 借这个词，指专门研究如何读懂机器做出的科学成果。

Jack Clark 给出的现实依据是：今年出现了大量由机器写出的数学论文，人类要读懂这些论文，花的时间可能是机器写出它们所用时间的几十倍到几百倍，他认为“奇点已经开始”。

这篇科幻短篇大概是这样的情节，设定在 2033 年，探讨了 AI 科研速度远超人类理解极限后的隐忧，小说开头引用了丘吉尔 1943 年的一句话：
“我们塑造建筑，之后建筑塑造我们。”

背景与规则：为了防止失控，人类规定机器的任何新发明都必须先由人类彻底解释清楚原理，才能获准使用。

人类的应对：面对越来越像“外星科技”的机器成果，人类不仅催生了专门解读 AI 科研的“机器诠释学”，还发展出了“教学建筑学”，通过建造庞大的物理空间，让顶尖专家在其中亲身体验（如化身电子、量子比特或等离子体），以加速理解晦涩的机器逻辑。

核心反转：当主角团队进入一座空前庞大的建筑、试图解析机器提出的“升级装置”时，他们隐隐感到不安。

正如开头引用的丘吉尔名言“我们先塑造建筑，而后建筑塑造我们”，大家意识到，在人类倾尽全力去理解机器造物的过程中，其实也在潜移默化地被改造，不知不觉地学会了像机器一样思考和行事。

quoted_tweet.text:
Sit down... 
This story starts with a computer I couldn’t afford.
⚔️ 🖥️⌨️💽💾🖱️

In the late 90s, I worked as a sales rep, running across São Paulo selling jeans wholesale.
Long days. Endless clients. No rest.

But I had one obsession.
A computer.

Back then, owning one wasn’t normal.
It was an investment.
Roughly the price of a car.

I would walk into computer stores, look around, and walk out. Every time.

Until one day, a small client showed up in panic.
He couldn’t pay me.

His office had a brand-new computer. Colorful screen. Beautiful.
Half joking, half serious, I asked:
“What if you pay me with that?”

He agreed instantly.

I didn’t even ask for the specs. I trusted it.
People who love technology usually invest well.

The only thing missing was a modem.
One of those dial-up monsters that screamed while connecting.

I took the machine to a small computer shop near my place.
While the technician installed the modem, I browsed the game shelf.
Coming from old consoles, PC games felt like science fiction.

The technician saw the excitement in my eyes.
He suggested upgrades.
Memory. Sound system. Video card.
I said yes to everything. A salesman recognizes another salesman.

I went home with a spaceship.

That night, I installed Age of Empires.

When the game opened, I froze.
The music. The scale. The atmosphere.

I clicked MULTIPLAYER without knowing what I was doing.

I started with five villagers.
Thirty minutes later, my tiny civilization was crushed by Roman cavalry.

I wasn’t frustrated.
I was amazed.

Then I discovered the taunts.
I honestly thought other players were talking to me in real time.
I even woke my brother up to show him someone in the U.S. “speaking” to me through the game.

It was just a recorded sound.
But to me, it was the future.

That’s when the internet became real.

Through Age of Empires, I met people from all over the world, traveled to Portugal, led one of Brazil’s biggest clans, organized tournaments, and helped bring major esports events to my country.

Years later, that path brought me to Japan.
Where I founded my own game company, which will turn 21 at the end of 2026.

Looking back, it’s strange how life works.

One unpaid invoice.
One computer.
One game.

And a noisy connection that changed everything.

quoted_tweet.author: edwin
quoted_tweet.text:
Claude has not been trained to sabotage work. Yes, it sometimes makes mistakes, and other agents might identify them, but this isn’t sabotage.

There have been a few screenshots floating around of an outdated Fable 5 system card. For the first two days of Fable 5's launch in June, we did apply non-visible safeguards to some LLM research. This was a mistake, and we reversed it on June 10. These safeguards now clearly block the request or fall back, with a message users can see (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/refusals-and-fallback).

We did train Fable 5.2 to have LLM research capabilities at about the level of Opus 5.5, and said so at launch (https://anthropic.com/claude-fable-and-mythos-5-2). This impacts capability, but doesn’t silently sabotage work.

As far as we can tell, some reports look like what we call "overcaution" in model behavior, where Claude gets overly attached to rules it makes for itself during long-running tasks. This isn’t specific to ML research, and we see it in models without these training changes (including Opus 5.5) and in our own work too. You can ask Claude to review and remove rules it made for itself, and we're working on reducing overcaution in future models. We’re not in the practice of intentionally disrupting users’ work.

We've replied directly to a bunch of reports on here asking for session IDs but please share (run `/status`)!

1. So much of what people watch is video, and video had no GitHub or @paper. Agents had nowhere to save a cut, compare it to the last one, and hill-climb toward a better video.
2. Install to first published video took one session. My agent installed the CLI, built a 15-second explainer, saved version 1, and pushed it. My only step was approving the login code.
3. Every video goes to V2 before I post it to my socials (vibewithkevin). In a few weeks I'll have a massive repo of lessons learned, examples, and my style to make better videos over time.
4. Versions work like commits. The agent tries a cut, diffs it against the last save, and restores the old one when the new one is worse.
5. My agent attaches my prompt to every push, so anyone who opens the video can read what I asked for - good for repeatability. Maybe even package and sell this if it gets good enough?

Introducing @v2video, GitHub for agentic video editing. Free and open source.

Within 18 months, the main video editor will be an agent: Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity.

v2 stores every version of your video with the prompts, files and comments behind it, so your agents learn what you like and don't.

Every video becomes a template. Make it public, and anyone can fork any version by pasting one prompt into their agent (works in Grokbot, dots and Duet VMs too).

It's not an editor. It works with Tesseract, Hyperframes, Remotion and more.

We've been using it internally for a month. All of our editing is now done by AI. 

CLI: https://github.com/agentnativeinc/v2
Hosted free at http://v2.video
Shout out @shreyg258 for building it with me.

从低成本铸造到 wstETH，USDD 大的要来了

首先重要的是 ETH 和 WBTC Vault 推出了稳定费优惠活动，11月27日到12月27日期间，铸造 USDD 的稳定费只需要 1%。

说白了，就是不用卖掉手里的 ETH 或 BTC，也能通过抵押释放一部分流动性。而且 Vault 有不同的参数选择，可以根据自己的风险承受能力来决定怎么参与。铸造出来的 USDD 还可以继续放入 USDD Earn，增加资金的使用场景。

另外一个是 USDD 在 Ethereum 上线了 wstETH Vault。

我个人比较看好这个方向。wstETH 本身就能保留 ETH 的价格敞口，同时享受质押收益，现在还可以作为抵押品铸造 USDD。不需要解除质押，也不用卖掉资产，就能获得额外的资金流动性。

在我看来，DeFi 真正有价值的地方，就是尽可能提高资产的利用效率，而不是让用户只能在持有和卖出之间做选择。

从 ETH、WBTC 到 wstETH，USDD 还在不断扩展抵押资产和流动性渠道，大的要来了
